title: The Blending Ratio Is Not Where the Performance Is:Diagnosing Prototype Blending for Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision–Language Models

paper.title: The Blending Ratio Is Not Where the Performance Is: Diagnosing Prototype Blending for Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision–Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Many few-shot adaptation methods for vision–language models classify with a convex combination of the zero-shot text prototype and the mean of the K K labelled image features, governed by a single blending ratio routinely tuned on held-out labels, often on the test set itself. This paper asks the question that the family’s own bias–variance justification invites: what is the right value of the blending ratio, can it be estimated without validation data, and is finding it actually where the performance is? We first show that the ratio minimising prototype mean-squared error has a closed form whose support-set plug-in is exactly a positive-part James–Stein coefficient shrinking towards the text prototype. Across a 4,800-cell matrix (ten datasets, five backbones including SigLIP, five shot counts, five seeds, four prompt tiers; the 5,000-cell grid minus 200 thin-pool drops) this theoretically optimal ratio is a reliable estimate of the wrong quantity: on the 950 950 cells of the primary prompt tier where it is defined it trails a test-set-oracle ratio by 8.5 8.5 accuracy points. It saturates at λ ≈ 1 \lambda\!\approx\!1 , discarding the text prior and reproducing a nearest-class-mean classifier, because 78 % 78\% of the text–image prototype distance it treats as bias is a class-independent offset that the arg max largely cancels. We prove the mechanism and measure its share of the damage by a counterfactual ( 26 % 26\% ). Second, a blend whose ratio is set by leave-one-out on the support set alone lands within 0.9 0.9 points of the oracle-ratio blend’s accuracy , so the ratio is estimable without validation data. Third, and most consequentially, validation-free linear probes beat even the oracle-tuned blend: CLAP by + 1.9 +1.9 points and LP++ by + 1.5 +1.5 on average, and at K ≥ 4 K{\geq}4 all four reproduced validation-free baselines sit above the oracle, the two linear probes by margins whose intervals exclude zero and that are invariant to solver precision. These results locate the family’s ceiling in its model class, not its hyperparameter: the blending ratio can be set near-optimally for free, and it is still not where the performance is. Code, cached features, and all per-cell records: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Liangzhi-Li/clipbench-blending .

C: mean accuracy, K ≥ 4 K\geq 4 , balanced cells: every reproduced validation-free baseline exceeds the test-set-oracle blend (dashed): the family is capacity-limited, not mis-tuned. Contrastively pre-trained vision–language models such as CLIP [ 1 ] , ALIGN [ 2 ] , and SigLIP [ 3 ] turned image classification into retrieval. Given a few labelled images per class, the natural upgrade averages each class’s K K image features into an image prototype and classifies by a convex combination of the two modalities, 𝒑 c ​ ( λ ) = λ ​ 𝝁 ^ c + ( 1 − λ ) ​ 𝒕 c \bm{p}_{c}(\lambda)=\lambda\,\hat{\bm{\mu}}_{c}+(1-\lambda)\,\bm{t}_{c} , with 𝒕 c \bm{t}_{c} the text prototype, 𝝁 ^ c \hat{\bm{\mu}}_{c} the empirical image prototype, and λ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \lambda\in[0,1] a blending ratio deciding how far to trust the few labelled shots over the frozen prior (Fig. 1 A). This underlies much of the few-shot adaptation literature: cache models blend zero-shot logits with support-set affinities [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , adapters residual with original features [ 8 ] , task-residual methods add a learned offset to the text prototype [ 9 ] , Gaussian discriminant heads blend generative with zero-shot logits [ 10 ] , training-free prototype methods the two modality means [ 11 , 12 ] . Each has a knob— α \alpha , λ \lambda , a residual ratio, a mixing coefficient—arbitrating between prior and evidence. How is that knob set? Almost never from the K K shots alone. The original Tip-Adapter searches its α \alpha and β \beta on the test set [ 4 ] ; the CoOp-inherited few-shot CLIP protocol [ 13 ] ships extra validation images that strict few-shot learning lacks; the official “hard-to-beat” GDA implementation [ 10 ] grid-searches its blending weight on held-out labels. A critical literature documents this: CLAP [ 14 ] showed state-of-the-art adapters need per-task tuning on large validation sets to beat a linear probe; LP++ [ 15 ] observed hyperparameters tuned “on the entire test set”; HOSO [ 16 ] formalised a validation-free protocol because most published numbers are not; benchmark critiques found the same pathology in test-time adaptation [ 17 ] and few-shot transfer [ 18 ] . The standard argument for blending, explicit in recent work [ 11 ] , is statistical: the image prototype is an unbiased, high-variance estimate of the true class mean, the text prototype a biased, zero-variance one; blending trades bias against variance. If that frame is right, three questions should have quantitative answers. First , what is the optimal blending ratio, and can it be computed rather than searched? Second , can it be estimated from the K K support shots alone, with no validation data? Third , the question nobody asks: if the ratio were set perfectly , would the classifier be competitive? We answer all three at scale: 4,800 cells (a 5,000-cell grid minus 200 guarded drops, Sec. V-D ) over ten datasets, five backbones, five shot counts, five support-set seeds, and four tiers of prompt quality, with four published validation-free baselines reproduced from official code and every comparison a paired difference with cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. (i) The theoretically optimal ratio is a reliable estimate of the wrong quantity. Minimising prototype mean-squared error yields a closed-form ratio whose support-set plug-in is exactly a positive-part James–Stein coefficient [ 19 , 20 ] shrinking the image prototype towards the text prototype—and provably dominating it at that objective (Prop. 3 ). Yet the classifier it induces trails a test-set-oracle ratio by 8.5 8.5 accuracy points on average and is statistically indistinguishable from zero-shot. The reason is structural: we measure 78.3 % 78.3\% [74.6, 82.1] of the squared text–image prototype distance as a class-independent offset, the modality gap [ 21 ] —one the arg max cancels but the MSE objective books as bias of the text prototype. On SigLIP the share rises to 86.6 % 86.6\% : the phenomenon belongs to contrastive pre-training at large, not to CLIP. (ii) The ratio is estimable without validation data. A leave-one-out estimator re-using all K K shots matches the test-set-oracle blend to within 0.9 0.9 accuracy points (ratio rank correlation 0.79 0.79 ) and responds correctly to interventions: upgrading the prompt from a generic template to LLM descriptions [ 22 ] lowers the oracle ratio, and the estimate tracks the shift. (iii) Even the oracle-tuned blend is not competitive. Validation-free linear probes beat the family’s own unreachable upper bound: CLAP by + 1.92 +1.92 [+0.87, +2.98] points and LP++ by + 1.46 +1.46 [+0.34, +2.58] on average. At K ≥ 4 K\geq 4 all four reproduced baselines are above the test-set-oracle blend in point estimate, three of them with intervals excluding zero. One caveat on scope: the Eq. ( 1 ) members we evaluate are our own constructions (Sec. VII-B ), so the bound concerns the family’s supremum, not any published system. We believe this reframes how the prototype-blending literature should be read (Sec. VII ): our results say the blending axis is worth at most the distance to the oracle, under one point for a well-estimated ratio, while the model-class gap to a plain linear probe on the same shots runs two to three points the other way. For practitioners this yields a validation-free recipe; for theory, it explains why the bias–variance story fails and supplies the decomposition that any future justification of blending will have to address. Contributions. (1) A closed form for the MSE-optimal blending ratio, identification of its support-set plug-in with positive-part James–Stein shrinkage, and its exact sampling theory (Prop. 4 ; Sec. III ). (2) A proof (Theorem 1 , Corollaries 1 – 2 ) and a 4,800-cell measurement that this ratio over-trusts image evidence by construction, because 78 % 78\% of the modality gap it penalises is class-independent and the arg max largely cancels (Secs. III , VI ; a counterfactual puts its share of the damage at 26 % 26\% ). (3) A leave-one-out ratio estimator using only the K K support shots, within 0.9 0.9 accuracy points of a test-set oracle, plus a rule making the published GDA baseline validation-free (Sec. IV ). (4) The capacity result, now with its theory: validation-free linear probes exceed the test-set-oracle blend (Sec. VI ), the blend path provably cannot reach the unrestricted separation a probe can aim at (Theorem 2 ), and the theorem’s predicted headroom picks out the strata where the measured surplus is largest. (5) A released benchmark—code, cached features, per-cell records, and line-by-line reproductions of CLAP, LP++, GDA, and HOSO—with paired statistics and a documented audit trail of every protocol decision (Sec. V ).

sections.heading: II-A Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision–Language Models
sections.text: Adapting a frozen vision–language model with K K labelled images per class has produced several method families. Prompt tuning learns continuous text-side context vectors (CoOp [ 13 ] , CoCoOp [ 23 ] , MaPLe [ 24 ] ), regularised to stay near the hand-crafted context [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] —the prior–evidence tension again, as a penalty rather than a ratio. Adapter methods attach lightweight modules on cached features: CLIP-Adapter blends a bottleneck MLP’s output with the original feature through a residual ratio [ 8 ] ; Task Residual adds a learned offset to the text prototypes [ 9 ] . Cache-based methods start from Tip-Adapter [ 4 ] , which adds an α \alpha -weighted support-set affinity term to the zero-shot logits; descendants refine the cache [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 28 , 29 ] , and kernel analyses unify the branch as regularised regression [ 30 , 31 ] . Generative heads blend fitted Gaussian-discriminant-analysis logits with the zero-shot logits [ 10 ] . Prototype methods blend the modality means directly [ 12 , 11 ] . Our subject cuts across these families: every one owns a scalar trading prior against evidence, and we analyse that scalar, not the architecture around it.

sections.heading: II-B Evaluation Protocols and the Validation-Set Problem
sections.text: The standard few-shot CLIP protocol inherited from CoOp quietly assumes labelled data beyond the K K shots. CLAP [ 14 ] showed that leading adapters outperform a linear probe only when tuned per task on a large validation set, and proposed a class-adaptive probe needing none. LP++ [ 15 ] derived data-driven step sizes from Lipschitz constants, making a strong linear probe without learning-rate search. HOSO [ 16 ] named the setting, validation-free few-shot adaptation, and fit CLIP-Adapter’s blending ratio on one held-out shot; the critique recurs in the medical domain [ 32 ] . At benchmark scale, Luo et al. [ 18 ] argue that cross-validation on K K shots is unreliable and reported rankings are dominated by hyperparameter access; Sheng et al. [ 17 ] re-evaluate test-time adaptation (a parallel line adapting without support labels [ 33 , 29 , 28 , 34 ] ) under equalised tuning and find most gains evaporate; Kravets et al. [ 35 ] show that CLIP’s pre-training corpus leaks class information into the benchmarks. Our work differs: rather than asking whether reported gains survive fair tuning, we bound what perfect tuning could ever deliver, and show the bound is below a validation-free linear probe.

sections.heading: II-C Shrinkage Estimation
sections.text: Shrinking a noisy mean towards a fixed target is a classical idea in statistics, running from Stein’s inadmissibility result [ 36 ] through the James–Stein estimator [ 19 ] to its empirical-Bayes reading and positive-part variant [ 20 , 37 ] . In classification it appears as nearest shrunken centroids [ 38 ] and, in few-shot learning, as prototype classifiers [ 39 ] with SimpleShot’s centre-then-normalise transform [ 40 ] ; our NCM baseline and centred variant are the VLM analogues of that line, except that the vector we subtract is a cross-modal offset rather than a within-modality mean. Ledoit–Wolf covariance shrinkage [ 41 ] appears inside the GDA baseline [ 10 ] , but it shrinks the covariance , not the prior–evidence ratio at issue here. In the VLM literature, Goswami et al. [ 11 ] recently derived the bias–variance decomposition of the blended prototype and observed empirically that the optimal mixing weight falls as shots decrease, but selected it by grid search against oracle statistics and, in their own words, still “require a validation set to tune the prototype mixing coefficient.” Sec. III completes that derivation and identifies the plug-in with positive-part James–Stein shrinkage. We claim no novelty for the estimator itself [ 37 ] , nor for the classical fact that bias and variance do not combine additively under 0 / 1 0/1 loss [ 42 , 43 ] ; what is new is the vision–language instantiation and its cause, together with the identification, its corollaries, and the measurement of the resulting cost. The class-independent component that breaks the MSE argument is the modality gap of Liang et al. [ 21 ] ; we appear to be the first to quantify its decision-time irrelevance for blended prototypes. Wider evidence agrees that the gap can be manipulated without tracking accuracy [ 44 , 21 , 45 ] , and the one few-shot entry uses a learned map rather than a subtraction [ 46 ] ; our centred variant (Sec. VI ) adds the missing few-shot data point. Weight-space interpolation [ 47 ] is a cousin of feature-space blending; we analyse the latter, which admits a closed form.

sections.heading: III The Blending Ratio in Theory
sections.text: We take the bias–variance justification of blending at face value, push it to its closed form (Sec. III-B ), quantify its estimation precision from K K shots (Sec. III-C ), then prove why this approach to optimisation was never the right goal (Sec. III-D ). The algebra is elementary; Sec. VI scores every prediction derived here.

sections.heading: IV-B Making GDA Validation-Free
sections.text: GDA [ 10 ] is described as training-free, but its official implementation grid-searches the weight α \alpha blending generative and zero-shot logits on a labelled validation set. We supply α \alpha by the same leave-one-out rule (the own-class Gaussian mean is refitted for each held-out sample, while the shared covariance, whose dependence on any single sample is O ⁡ ( 1 / N ) O(1/N) , is kept fixed), yielding a validation-free GDA that closes about half the gap to the validation-tuned version at K ∈ { 2 , 4 } K\in\{2,4\} and none of it at K ≥ 8 K\geq 8 (Table IV ).

sections.heading: IV-C Reference Points That Use Forbidden Data
sections.text: The quantities below anchor the analysis from above, always as bounds, never as methods. The accuracy-oracle ratio grid-searches a single global λ \lambda on the test labels—the best the family’s contested hyperparameter can possibly deliver. The MSE-oracle ratio evaluates Eq. ( 5 ) per class with 𝝁 ∗ , 𝚺 ∗ \bm{\mu}^{*},\bm{\Sigma}^{*} estimated from pool data outside the support set, isolating objective error from estimation error. And Tip-Adapter with α , β \alpha,\beta tuned on the test set reproduces the family’s historical practice [ 4 ] . The accuracy oracle is deliberately global: a per-class oracle would fit C C free parameters to the test labels (overfitting, not a bound), and Sec. VI-G measures exactly how much of its apparent gain that is.

sections.heading: V-A Datasets and Splits
sections.text: We use ten classification datasets (Table I ): FGVC-Aircraft [ 51 ] , Caltech101 [ 52 ] , Stanford Cars [ 53 ] , DTD [ 54 ] , EuroSAT [ 55 ] , Flowers102 [ 56 ] , Food-101 [ 57 ] , ImageNet [ 58 ] , Oxford-IIIT Pets [ 59 ] , and SUN397 [ 60 ] . Images, class names, and zero-shot prompt templates come from the publicly pinned clip-benchmark webdataset distributions, whose zero-shot numbers our sanity gate (below) verifies against that project’s public results. Deviations from the CoOp-lineage protocol [ 13 ] : (i) splits are clip-benchmark’s, not CoOp’s split_zhou files, so absolute numbers are not cell-comparable with that lineage—every method here sees identical splits, as our claims require; (ii) ImageNet and SUN397 ship only evaluation shards, so we form a deterministic per-class 68/32 pool/test split (seeded once, before any experiment ran); (iii) the clip-benchmark Caltech101 is the 102-class VTAB variant whose literal background class no prompt can name, placing zero-shot ∼ 4 {\sim}4 points below 101-class numbers (a protocol difference, not an extraction bug); (iv) Flowers102’s pool holds ten images per class, capping it at K ≤ 4 K\leq 4 ; (v) UCF101 has no clip-benchmark distribution and is omitted. Support sampling. For each (dataset, backbone, K K , seed) cell, K K shots per class are drawn from the pool with one of five seeds; all methods in a cell see the identical support set, making every comparison paired. Population statistics for the MSE-oracle come from the pool minus the support set, so oracle and estimate never share samples. Test data is touched only by final evaluation and the explicitly-labelled oracles.

sections.heading: V-B Backbones and Text Priors
sections.text: Five backbones: OpenAI CLIP RN50, ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14, and SigLIP ViT-B/16 [ 3 ] via OpenCLIP [ 61 ] , all frozen, features ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalised once and cached; SigLIP’s different pre-training objective tests whether the diagnosis is CLIP-specific. Four text-prior tiers per dataset: the generic photo template (“a photo of a {}.”), the dataset-specific template, the full clip-benchmark prompt ensemble , and CuPL -style LLM descriptions [ 22 , 62 ] generated with gpt-4.1-mini (three query templates for each of the 2,092 classes; prompts and outputs released), cleaned, class-name-prefixed when absent, encoded per sentence, and averaged into a unit-norm prototype, applied uniformly across datasets and text encoders. The four tiers instrument the prior-quality axis of Table II .

sections.heading: V-C Methods
sections.text: Fifteen classifiers are evaluated on the dataset-specific tier. Eleven are validation-free (zero-shot, NCM, four blends, GDA at α = 1 \alpha{=}1 and by LOO, HOSO, CLAP, LP++), and four consume data a deployed system would not have (Sec. IV : the MSE-oracle and accuracy-oracle ratios, Tip-Adapter’s test-tuned ( α , β ) (\alpha,\beta) , and GDA’s validation-tuned α \alpha ); the released records log, per cell, which quantity each method selected and from which split. Validation-free methods: zero-shot; NCM (image prototypes); the James–Stein blend of Eq. ( 7 ) and its 𝚫 \bm{\Delta} -centred variant; the LOO blend with and without K K -correction; GDA with α = 1 \alpha{=}1 and with α \alpha by LOO; and three published baselines—CLAP [ 14 ] , LP++ [ 15 ] , HOSO [ 16 ] —re-implemented on cached features from their official code line by line (HOSO from its paper; no code exists). Our GDA and LP++ agree with the official implementations to relative error 10 − 8 10^{-8} on identical inputs. Unavoidable deviations, disclosed: no baseline uses image augmentation here (features are cached once; official CLAP averages 20 augmented views, GDA uses 10 augmentation epochs; this hurts GDA most, whose covariance degenerates at K = 1 K{=}1 , where we report it as zero-shot); CLAP’s anchor scale, unrecoverable from normalised caches, is fixed at its typical value 10 10 ; LP++’s optional early-epoch selection on an extra validation split is disabled (its validation-free path, the paper’s stated intent).

sections.heading: V-D Statistics and the Combination Guard
sections.text: Every accuracy difference is computed within cells (identical support sets) and aggregated by a cluster bootstrap whose resampling unit is the dataset (10,000 resamples). Cells sharing a dataset share a test split, pool, vocabulary and text prior; resampling the 4,800 cells individually would shrink every interval by roughly an order of magnitude. The intervals therefore answer “would this survive another draw of datasets ”; n n counts cells, the effective sample size is the ten clusters. Ten is few enough that the percentile interval cannot be assumed honest, so we measured it: a variance-matched simulation puts nominal- 95 % 95\% percentile coverage at 89.3 % 89.3\% . We therefore report Student- t t intervals on the bootstrap standard error ( G − 1 = 9 G-1=9 df), which the same simulation puts at 93.7 93.7 – 94.8 % 94.8\% ; every interval here is the wider, corrected one ( code/boot_coverage.py ). No multiplicity correction is applied across the roughly thirty intervals reported; discount lower bounds within a few tenths of zero accordingly—the two closest calls are HOSO’s K ≥ 4 K{\geq}4 margin (Table V , lower bound + 0.01 +0.01 ) and CLAP’s SigLIP margin (Table VI , + 0.11 +0.11 ). By- K K aggregates are restricted to the 45 dataset × \times backbone combinations present at every K K ; without this guard, dropped cells masquerade as trends. Cells whose per-class pool residue after support sampling falls below five are dropped and counted (200 of 5,000, all Flowers102 at K ∈ { 8 , 16 } K\in\{8,16\} ).

sections.heading: VI-A The Theoretically Optimal Ratio Fails
sections.text: By Sec. III the James–Stein blend estimates its own target well (per-class λ ^ \hat{\lambda} vs. pool-estimated λ ∗ \lambda^{*} : MAE 0.007 0.007 ), and by Prop. 3 it dominates the raw prototype at that target. The classifier it induces nonetheless fails: averaged over all cells it trails the test-set-oracle ratio by − 8.51 -8.51 [-12.99, -4.04] ( n = 950 n{=}950 cells in 10 10 dataset clusters) and its pooled advantage over zero-shot is − 0.12 -0.12 [-8.99, +8.75]—an average over a sign change, not an equivalence: 10.7 10.7 pp below zero-shot at K = 2 K{=}2 and 6.6 6.6 pp above at K = 16 K{=}16 (Table IV ). The MSE-oracle (Eq. ( 5 ) at population statistics) confirms objective error: 64.1 % 64.1\% mean accuracy against the accuracy-oracle’s 72.8 % 72.8\% (Table IV , K ≥ 2 K\geq 2 ). The consequence is blunt: at λ ^ ≈ 1 \hat{\lambda}\!\approx\!1 the MSE-optimal rule is, empirically, the nearest-class-mean classifier—beating NCM by + 0.76 +0.76 [+0.38, +1.13], against NCM’s own − 9.27 -9.27 [-14.11, -4.42] to the oracle ratio. The closed form’s entire content is that it discards the text prior , at the long-known cost in accuracy; what is new is that the family’s own derivation leads there. Fig. 3 shows the mechanism: James–Stein ratios crowd the top of the plot (mean 0.96 0.96 ) wherever the accuracy-optimal ratio lies (mean 0.33 0.33 ); Fig. 2 shows the curve: a broad plateau, then a cliff near λ = 1 \lambda{=}1 , exactly where Eq. sections.heading: VI-H Two Protocol Objections, Measured
sections.text: Both are answered with the released caches rather than argument. Augmentation. Our baselines run on features cached once, while the official CLAP/GDA/LP++/HOSO recipes all consume augmented views. We restored each recipe on a seeded 20-view cache of the support images (817 paired cells, identical draws and test sets; 39 of the 50 pairs, all 10 datasets). The effect is nil for CLAP ( − 0.08 -0.08 [-0.52, +0.36]) and unresolved for LP++ ( − 0.98 -0.98 [-2.13, +0.18]), a point estimate that at face value thins but does not erase its oracle margins (Table V ); HOSO moves + 0.28 +0.28 [+0.04, +0.52], inside its precision band. GDA is the exception, in the unexpected direction: augmentation costs it − 18.83 -18.83 [-30.66, -6.99] at K = 1 K{=}1 (a covariance from ten crops of one image is worse than the degenerate fallback) and gains + 4.28 +4.28 [+1.19, +7.36] at K = 2 K{=}2 . Splits. Our splits are clip-benchmark’s, not the split_zhou files of the CoOp lineage, so our absolute numbers are not comparable with that literature’s tables. Re-extracting on the CoOp splits (349 cells; 23 of the 50 pairs of its own ten-dataset grid, all five backbones appearing, ViT-B/16 on every dataset; UCF101 included, ImageNet excluded, as its CoOp protocol needs the full train set) reproduces every qualitative finding: CLAP exceeds the test-set-oracle blending ratio by + 2.26 +2.26 [+1.04, +3.49], the LOO blend sits − 1.64 -1.64 [-2.93, -0.35] below it, the James–Stein blend − 7.68 -7.68 [-13.70, -1.67], and the class-independent share of the prototype distance is 80.3 % 80.3\% [74.8, 85.8]. Modern encoders. Two 240-cell arms on the full grid ask whether any of this is an artefact of 2021-vintage CLIP. On SigLIP2-B/16 [ 63 ] , findings (i) and (ii) reproduce outright ( λ ^ \hat{\lambda} saturates at 0.97 against an accuracy-optimal 0.30), and the capacity finding holds through CLAP, which clears the oracle ratio by + 1.29 +1.29 [+0.17, +2.42]. LP++ attenuates: + 1.50 +1.50 [-0.22, +3.22] at K ≥ 4 K{\geq}4 against the published + 2.78 +2.78 , and − 0.16 -0.16 [-1.45, +1.14] over all K K (dragged by K = 1 K{=}1 ); these are intervals a single backbone cannot resolve, so on this encoder the probe half of the headline rests on CLAP. The sharper arm is text-free: DINOv3-B/16 [ 64 ] ( 86 86 M parameters, matching ViT-B/16) has no text tower, hence no text prototype and no blending ratio, so it can enter only as a probe-side reference. A plain logistic probe on its features beats the family’s test-set oracle by + 7.21 +7.21 [+0.41, +14.01] at K ≥ 4 K{\geq}4 , while the identical probe on CLIP features does not ( − 2.24 -2.24 [-6.25, +1.76]): the ceiling of Sec. VI-C is a property of the blending family (Theorem 2 ), not of CLIP’s feature space (per- K K tables and protocol in the supplement).

Prompt tier : repeating the λ \lambda -family analyses on the photo, ensemble and CuPL tiers changes levels but no orderings (oracle-vs-LOO gap under a point on every tier; gap share moves two points): the geometry that defeats MSE shrinkage belongs to the encoders, not the prompt. Re-running both probes against each tier’s own test-set-oracle ratio (3,600 paired cells, the full 10-dataset grid) leaves every contrast positive, intervals excluding zero: CLAP + 2.11 +2.11 [+1.21, +3.01] on the photo template, + 1.85 +1.85 [+0.85, +2.86] on the ensemble and + 1.67 +1.67 [+0.73, +2.60] on CuPL, LP++ + 1.86 +1.86 [+0.82, +2.89], + 1.28 +1.28 [+0.21, +2.34] and + 1.28 +1.28 [+0.22, +2.33]. The margin shrinks monotonically as the prior improves—a better prototype is worth more to the blend than to the probe—but three tiers of it do not close the gap. Strata : the headline CLAP-vs-oracle contrast is positive in 43 43 of 50 50 dataset × \times backbone strata; the seven exceptions are four Flowers102 strata and three near-ceiling cases, all within 0.3 0.3 pp of zero—inside median seed noise ( 0.4 0.4 pp).

sections.heading: VII-A How to Read the Blending Literature Now
sections.text: Blending is not useless. The LOO blend beats zero-shot by 7.6 7.6 pp and never harms a strong prior, but a one-or-two-point gain over a predecessor, tuned on forbidden labels, lies inside a band free leave-one-out already spans, and wholly below a validation-free probe. New blends should be benchmarked against their family’s test-set-oracle ratio and against CLAP or LP++ on identical shots, separating “a better mechanism” from “a better-tuned ratio”—which current evaluation culture [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] does not. This sharpens critiques [ 18 , 17 , 35 ] that hyperparameter access inflates few-shot gains, adding an existence bound: with unlimited access on its central hyperparameter, the family is still dominated. LOO also removes the excuse that validation-free selection of such scalars is impossible [ 18 ] .

sections.heading: VII-B Scope of the Claim
sections.text: The bound covers Eq. ( 1 ), one global interpolation coefficient between the two modality prototype sets, under cosine similarity. It excludes accuracy-tuned per-class coefficients (unbounded test-set overfitting), logit blends with per-branch temperatures and, strictly, sample-level cache models, including Tip-Adapter, whose test-tuned instance we report anyway, and which also falls below the probes (Table IV ). The members we evaluate are our own constructions (Sec. I ): published methods in this exact form tune the ratio on forbidden data or fold it into a larger head. The bound is on the family and tight by construction: no member beats the test-set-oracle ratio, which is itself beaten. We do not claim linear probes are optimal, only that they are the cheapest widely-available class exceeding the family’s supremum. The bound is empirical, with Theorem 2 as its model-level counterpart: in the Gaussian idealisation the family’s ceiling is the plane-restricted Mahalanobis separation, and the headroom it implies predicts where the measured surplus is largest. Across ten domains, three orders of magnitude in class count, and six encoders, no counterexample appeared.

sections.heading: VII-C Why the Bias–Variance Story Misleads, and What Could Rescue It
sections.text: The MSE argument fails quantitatively, not conceptually: blending is shrinkage, but towards a target whose offset is 78 % 78\% decision-irrelevant, under a loss that cannot tell. Corollary 2 gives the correct two-class objective and its solution; its multi-class, estimable form is open. A decision-theoretic shrinkage would target the pairwise differences 𝒕 c − 𝒕 c ′ \bm{t}_{c}-\bm{t}_{c^{\prime}} (Theorem 1 ); our centred variant, the zeroth-order attempt, failed, showing the correction must be anisotropic, not scalar. An anisotropic or subspace shrinkage would estimate which gap directions are decision-relevant, as in the text-aligned projections of [ 11 ] , but Eq. ( 16 ) needs exactly the quantities ( 𝒖 \bm{u} , 𝜹 \bm{\delta} ) that K K shots estimate worst. Until either exists, Eq. ( 7 ) is a cautionary identity: the most principled-looking closed form here is a positive-part James–Stein rule, and it is precisely wrong. The released records also support oracle-bounding other tuned scalars (TTA temperatures [ 33 , 17 ] , interpolation coefficients [ 47 ] , cache sizes [ 29 , 28 ] ), several of which we suspect matter as little.

sections.heading: VII-D Recommendations for Practice
sections.text: (1) K ≥ 2 K\geq 2 shots, no validation data: train CLAP or LP++ on cached features—validation-free, precision-stable, better than every blend we could construct or bound. (2) Blend required anyway: set the ratio by Algorithm 1 , never on labels the deployment will not have; expect to lose two to three points against a probe. (3) K = 1 K{=}1 : use CLAP or stay zero-shot; do not blend. (4) Evaluating a method that owns a trust parameter: report that parameter’s test-set-oracle value alongside it. (5) Optimal trust shifts with prior quality (Table II ); a ratio tuned under one prompt tier silently mis-tunes under another, whereas LOO re-adapts by construction.

sections.heading: VII-E Limitations
sections.text: What this study does not establish. (i) Our splits are clip-benchmark’s, so absolute numbers are not comparable with CoOp-lineage tables; the CoOp-split replication (Sec. VI-H ) shows the conclusions transfer, not the levels. (ii) The augmentation and split arms subsample the grid; their intervals lean on the covered clusters. (iii) HOSO, re-implemented from its paper (no public code), is the one precision-sensitive method; its comparisons carry a ∼ 0.5 {\sim}0.5 pp band. (iv) CLAP’s anchor scale is fixed rather than recovered. (v) The per-class accuracy oracle (Sec. VI-G ) is a multi-start coordinate ascent, not a certified optimum, and its split-half version is ViT-B/16 only. (vi) Pre-training contamination [ 35 ] affects all methods equally but is not corrected for. (vii) Flowers102 stops at K = 4 K{=}4 and UCF101 is absent. (viii) Our scope is single-label classification from cached global features. None of these, in our judgement, threatens the three findings, which rest on paired within-cell comparisons that these factors shift jointly rather than differentially.

sections.heading: VIII Conclusion
sections.text: We set out with a simple question: how much is the blending ratio at the heart of few-shot vision–language adaptation actually worth? Across 4,800 paired comparisons, we found the answer to be remarkably consistent. The model family’s own bias–variance argument leads to a positive-part James–Stein rule, but that rule optimises prototype error rather than classification, and 78 % 78\% of the bias it seeks to correct is decision-irrelevant. The ratio that accuracy actually prefers can be estimated from the support set alone. We validated this through leave-one-out, to within one point of a test-set oracle, removing the need to tune on held-out or forbidden labels. Importantly, even the oracle-tuned blend is beaten by validation-free linear probes. The bottleneck is therefore not how one chooses the blending ratio. The findings suggest a rethink on hyperparameters. The ratio is not an unresolved tuning problem. It can be estimated accurately. Our observation is that the literature has been placing its efforts on precisely this optimisation, while the key question is whether the model family itself is best suited to the task at hand. Future work should reconsider whether simple prototype blending is an adequate adaptation mechanism at all.

Abstract Many few-shot adaptation methods for vision–language models classify with a convex combination of the zero-shot text prototype and the mean of the K K labelled image features, governed by a single blending ratio routinely tuned on held-out labels, often on the test set itself. This paper asks the question that the family’s own bias–variance justification invites: what is the right value of the blending ratio, can it be estimated without validation data, and is finding it actually where the performance is? We first show that the ratio minimising prototype mean-squared error has a closed form whose support-set plug-in is exactly a positive-part James–Stein coefficient shrinking towards the text prototype. Across a 4,800-cell matrix (ten datasets, five backbones including SigLIP, five shot counts, five seeds, four prompt tiers; the 5,000-cell grid minus 200 thin-pool drops) this theoretically optimal ratio is a reliable estimate of the wrong quantity: on the 950 950 cells of the primary prompt tier where it is defined it trails a test-set-oracle ratio by 8.5 8.5 accuracy points. It saturates at λ ≈ 1 \lambda\!\approx\!1 , discarding the text prior and reproducing a nearest-class-mean classifier, because 78 % 78\% of the text–image prototype distance it treats as bias is a class-independent offset that the arg max largely cancels. We prove the mechanism and measure its share of the damage by a counterfactual ( 26 % 26\% ). Second, a blend whose ratio is set by leave-one-out on the support set alone lands within 0.9 0.9 points of the oracle-ratio blend’s accuracy , so the ratio is estimable without validation data. Third, and most consequentially, validation-free linear probes beat even the oracle-tuned blend: CLAP by + 1.9 +1.9 points and LP++ by + 1.5 +1.5 on average, and at K ≥ 4 K{\geq}4 all four reproduced validation-free baselines sit above the oracle, the two linear probes by margins whose intervals exclude zero and that are invariant to solver precision. These results locate the family’s ceiling in its model class, not its hyperparameter: the blending ratio can be set near-optimally for free, and it is still not where the performance is. Code, cached features, and all per-cell records: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Liangzhi-Li/clipbench-blending . Index Terms: Vision–language models, CLIP, few-shot learning, transfer learning, shrinkage estimation, James–Stein, model selection, evaluation protocols. I Introduction Fig. 1: A: PCA of the prototype geometry (Pets, ViT-B/16): the common offset 𝚫 \bm{\Delta} (the modality gap) is 75 % 75\% of the squared text–image prototype distance here, yet costs far less at decision time (Thm. 1 ; Sec. VI-G ). Blending slides each prototype along its dotted path; marks are the two objectives’ choices. B: measured accuracy and prototype MSE vs. λ \lambda (Food-101, K = 4 K{=}4 ): the MSE minimum ( λ ≈ 0.96 \lambda\approx 0.96 , where Eq. ( 7 ) sits) costs 14.2 14.2 accuracy points against the accuracy peak ( λ ≈ 0.09 \lambda\approx 0.09 , which leave-one-out finds). C: mean accuracy, K ≥ 4 K\geq 4 , balanced cells: every reproduced validation-free baseline exceeds the test-set-oracle blend (dashed): the family is capacity-limited, not mis-tuned. Contrastively pre-trained vision–language models such as CLIP [ 1 ] , ALIGN [ 2 ] , and SigLIP [ 3 ] turned image classification into retrieval. Given a few labelled images per class, the natural upgrade averages each class’s K K image features into an image prototype and classifies by a convex combination of the two modalities, 𝒑 c ​ ( λ ) = λ ​ 𝝁 ^ c + ( 1 − λ ) ​ 𝒕 c \bm{p}_{c}(\lambda)=\lambda\,\hat{\bm{\mu}}_{c}+(1-\lambda)\,\bm{t}_{c} , with 𝒕 c \bm{t}_{c} the text prototype, 𝝁 ^ c \hat{\bm{\mu}}_{c} the empirical image prototype, and λ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \lambda\in[0,1] a blending ratio deciding how far to trust the few labelled shots over the frozen prior (Fig. 1 A). This underlies much of the few-shot adaptation literature: cache models blend zero-shot logits with support-set affinities [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , adapters residual with original features [ 8 ] , task-residual methods add a learned offset to the text prototype [ 9 ] , Gaussian discriminant heads blend generative with zero-shot logits [ 10 ] , training-free prototype methods the two modality means [ 11 , 12 ] . Each has a knob— α \alpha , λ \lambda , a residual ratio, a mixing coefficient—arbitrating between prior and evidence. How is that knob set? Almost never from the K K shots alone. The original Tip-Adapter searches its α \alpha and β \beta on the test set [ 4 ] ; the CoOp-inherited few-shot CLIP protocol [ 13 ] ships extra validation images that strict few-shot learning lacks; the official “hard-to-beat” GDA implementation [ 10 ] grid-searches its blending weight on held-out labels. A critical literature documents this: CLAP [ 14 ] showed state-of-the-art adapters need per-task tuning on large validation sets to beat a linear probe; LP++ [ 15 ] observed hyperparameters tuned “on the entire test set”; HOSO [ 16 ] formalised a validation-free protocol because most published numbers are not; benchmark critiques found the same pathology in test-time adaptation [ 17 ] and few-shot transfer [ 18 ] . The standard argument for blending, explicit in recent work [ 11 ] , is statistical: the image prototype is an unbiased, high-variance estimate of the true class mean, the text prototype a biased, zero-variance one; blending trades bias against variance. If that frame is right, three questions should have quantitative answers. First , what is the optimal blending ratio, and can it be computed rather than searched? Second , can it be estimated from the K K support shots alone, with no validation data? Third , the question nobody asks: if the ratio were set perfectly , would the classifier be competitive? We answer all three at scale: 4,800 cells (a 5,000-cell grid minus 200 guarded drops, Sec. V-D ) over ten datasets, five backbones, five shot counts, five support-set seeds, and four tiers of prompt quality, with four published validation-free baselines reproduced from official code and every comparison a paired difference with cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. (i) The theoretically optimal ratio is a reliable estimate of the wrong quantity. Minimising prototype mean-squared error yields a closed-form ratio whose support-set plug-in is exactly a positive-part James–Stein coefficient [ 19 , 20 ] shrinking the image prototype towards the text prototype—and provably dominating it at that objective (Prop. 3 ). Yet the classifier it induces trails a test-set-oracle ratio by 8.5 8.5 accuracy points on average and is statistically indistinguishable from zero-shot. The reason is structural: we measure 78.3 % 78.3\% [74.6, 82.1] of the squared text–image prototype distance as a class-independent offset, the modality gap [ 21 ] —one the arg max cancels but the MSE objective books as bias of the text prototype. On SigLIP the share rises to 86.6 % 86.6\% : the phenomenon belongs to contrastive pre-training at large, not to CLIP. (ii) The ratio is estimable without validation data. A leave-one-out estimator re-using all K K shots matches the test-set-oracle blend to within 0.9 0.9 accuracy points (ratio rank correlation 0.79 0.79 ) and responds correctly to interventions: upgrading the prompt from a generic template to LLM descriptions [ 22 ] lowers the oracle ratio, and the estimate tracks the shift. (iii) Even the oracle-tuned blend is not competitive. Validation-free linear probes beat the family’s own unreachable upper bound: CLAP by + 1.92 +1.92 [+0.87, +2.98] points and LP++ by + 1.46 +1.46 [+0.34, +2.58] on average. At K ≥ 4 K\geq 4 all four reproduced baselines are above the test-set-oracle blend in point estimate, three of them with intervals excluding zero. One caveat on scope: the Eq. ( 1 ) members we evaluate are our own constructions (Sec. VII-B ), so the bound concerns the family’s supremum, not any published system. We believe this reframes how the prototype-blending literature should be read (Sec. VII ): our results say the blending axis is worth at most the distance to the oracle, under one point for a well-estimated ratio, while the model-class gap to a plain linear probe on the same shots runs two to three points the other way. For practitioners this yields a validation-free recipe; for theory, it explains why the bias–variance story fails and supplies the decomposition that any future justification of blending will have to address. Contributions. (1) A closed form for the MSE-optimal blending ratio, identification of its support-set plug-in with positive-part James–Stein shrinkage, and its exact sampling theory (Prop. 4 ; Sec. III ). (2) A proof (Theorem 1 , Corollaries 1 – 2 ) and a 4,800-cell measurement that this ratio over-trusts image evidence by construction, because 78 % 78\% of the modality gap it penalises is class-independent and the arg max largely cancels (Secs. III , VI ; a counterfactual puts its share of the damage at 26 % 26\% ). (3) A leave-one-out ratio estimator using only the K K support shots, within 0.9 0.9 accuracy points of a test-set oracle, plus a rule making the published GDA baseline validation-free (Sec. IV ). (4) The capacity result, now with its theory: validation-free linear probes exceed the test-set-oracle blend (Sec. VI ), the blend path provably cannot reach the unrestricted separation a probe can aim at (Theorem 2 ), and the theorem’s predicted headroom picks out the strata where the measured surplus is largest. (5) A released benchmark—code, cached features, per-cell records, and line-by-line reproductions of CLAP, LP++, GDA, and HOSO—with paired statistics and a documented audit trail of every protocol decision (Sec. V ). II Related Work II-A Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision–Language Models Adapting a frozen vision–language model with K K labelled images per class has produced several method families. Prompt tuning learns continuous text-side context vectors (CoOp [ 13 ] , CoCoOp [ 23 ] , MaPLe [ 24 ] ), regularised to stay near the hand-crafted context [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] —the prior–evidence tension again, as a penalty rather than a ratio. Adapter methods attach lightweight modules on cached features: CLIP-Adapter blends a bottleneck MLP’s output with the original feature through a residual ratio [ 8 ] ; Task Residual adds a learned offset to the text prototypes [ 9 ] . Cache-based methods start from Tip-Adapter [ 4 ] , which adds an α \alpha -weighted support-set affinity term to the zero-shot logits; descendants refine the cache [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 28 , 29 ] , and kernel analyses unify the branch as regularised regression [ 30 , 31 ] . Generative heads blend fitted Gaussian-discriminant-analysis logits with the zero-shot logits [ 10 ] . Prototype methods blend the modality means directly [ 12 , 11 ] . Our subject cuts across these families: every one owns a scalar trading prior against evidence, and we analyse that scalar, not the architecture around it. II-B Evaluation Protocols and the Validation-Set Problem The standard few-shot CLIP protocol inherited from CoOp quietly assumes labelled data beyond the K K shots. CLAP [ 14 ] showed that leading adapters outperform a linear probe only when tuned per task on a large validation set, and proposed a class-adaptive probe needing none. LP++ [ 15 ] derived data-driven step sizes from Lipschitz constants, making a strong linear probe without learning-rate search. HOSO [ 16 ] named the setting, validation-free few-shot adaptation, and fit CLIP-Adapter’s blending ratio on one held-out shot; the critique recurs in the medical domain [ 32 ] . At benchmark scale, Luo et al. [ 18 ] argue that cross-validation on K K shots is unreliable and reported rankings are dominated by hyperparameter access; Sheng et al. [ 17 ] re-evaluate test-time adaptation (a parallel line adapting without support labels [ 33 , 29 , 28 , 34 ] ) under equalised tuning and find most gains evaporate; Kravets et al. [ 35 ] show that CLIP’s pre-training corpus leaks class information into the benchmarks. Our work differs: rather than asking whether reported gains survive fair tuning, we bound what perfect tuning could ever deliver, and show the bound is below a validation-free linear probe. II-C Shrinkage Estimation Shrinking a noisy mean towards a fixed target is a classical idea in statistics, running from Stein’s inadmissibility result [ 36 ] through the James–Stein estimator [ 19 ] to its empirical-Bayes reading and positive-part variant [ 20 , 37 ] . In classification it appears as nearest shrunken centroids [ 38 ] and, in few-shot learning, as prototype classifiers [ 39 ] with SimpleShot’s centre-then-normalise transform [ 40 ] ; our NCM baseline and centred variant are the VLM analogues of that line, except that the vector we subtract is a cross-modal offset rather than a within-modality mean. Ledoit–Wolf covariance shrinkage [ 41 ] appears inside the GDA baseline [ 10 ] , but it shrinks the covariance , not the prior–evidence ratio at issue here. In the VLM literature, Goswami et al. [ 11 ] recently derived the bias–variance decomposition of the blended prototype and observed empirically that the optimal mixing weight falls as shots decrease, but selected it by grid search against oracle statistics and, in their own words, still “require a validation set to tune the prototype mixing coefficient.” Sec. III completes that derivation and identifies the plug-in with positive-part James–Stein shrinkage. We claim no novelty for the estimator itself [ 37 ] , nor for the classical fact that bias and variance do not combine additively under 0 / 1 0/1 loss [ 42 , 43 ] ; what is new is the vision–language instantiation and its cause, together with the identification, its corollaries, and the measurement of the resulting cost. The class-independent component that breaks the MSE argument is the modality gap of Liang et al. [ 21 ] ; we appear to be the first to quantify its decision-time irrelevance for blended prototypes. Wider evidence agrees that the gap can be manipulated without tracking accuracy [ 44 , 21 , 45 ] , and the one few-shot entry uses a learned map rather than a subtraction [ 46 ] ; our centred variant (Sec. VI ) adds the missing few-shot data point. Weight-space interpolation [ 47 ] is a cousin of feature-space blending; we analyse the latter, which admits a closed form. III The Blending Ratio in Theory We take the bias–variance justification of blending at face value, push it to its closed form (Sec. III-B ), quantify its estimation precision from K K shots (Sec.
